cpp-basics.title: Compile and run a first program
cpp-basics.explanation: Turn on warnings (-Wall -Wextra) from day one; the compiler catches many mistakes before they become bugs.

cpp-types.title: Integer overflow and safe conversion
cpp-types.explanation: Signed overflow is undefined behaviour; unsigned arithmetic wraps. Use fixed-width types when size matters and static_cast to make conversions visible.

cpp-control-functions.title: Pass by value, reference and const reference
cpp-control-functions.code:
void byValue(std::string s)        { s += "!"; }   // copies; caller unchanged
void byRef(std::string& s)         { s += "!"; }   // modifies caller's string
std::size_t len(const std::string& s) { return s.size(); } // no copy, read-only

std::string msg = "hi";
byValue(msg);  // msg == "hi"
byRef(msg);    // msg == "hi!"
cpp-control-functions.explanation: Pass large objects by const reference to avoid copies, and use a non-const reference only when the function is meant to change the argument.

cpp-pointers.title: Dangling pointer
cpp-pointers.explanation: Returning the address of a local variable leaves a dangling pointer; reading it is undefined behaviour. Return by value or a smart pointer instead.

cpp-oop.title: Virtual functions and a virtual destructor
cpp-oop.explanation: override lets the compiler check the signature, and the virtual destructor ensures Circle's destructor runs when deleted through a Shape pointer.

cpp-stl.title: Algorithms instead of loops
cpp-stl.explanation: Standard algorithms are tested and state intent clearly. The erase-remove idiom (or C++20 std::erase_if) is how you delete matching elements from a vector.

cpp-raii.title: RAII file handle and lock
cpp-raii.explanation: Resources tied to object lifetimes are released on every exit path, including exceptions, with no cleanup code to forget.

cpp-modern-templates.title: A constrained template (C++20 concepts)
cpp-modern-templates.explanation: Concepts state requirements up front, so misuse produces a short, readable error instead of pages of template instantiation messages.

cpp-safety.title: Catch memory bugs with sanitizers
cpp-safety.code:
$ g++ -std=c++20 -g -fsanitize=address,undefined bug.cpp -o bug && ./bug
==1234==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow on address 0x602000000014
WRITE of size 4 at 0x602000000014 thread T0
    #0 0x401234 in main bug.cpp:7
cpp-safety.explanation: AddressSanitizer and UBSan turn silent memory corruption into an exact file and line. Run tests with them in CI; prefer std::vector::at, std::span and smart pointers in code.

docker-basics.title: Image vs container
docker-basics.code:
$ docker pull nginx:1.27            # download an image (read-only template)
$ docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx:1.27   # start a container from it
$ docker ps
CONTAINER ID  IMAGE       STATUS        PORTS                  NAMES
3f1c2a...     nginx:1.27  Up 5 seconds  0.0.0.0:8080->80/tcp   web
$ docker stop web && docker rm web
docker-basics.explanation: One image can start many containers. Removing a container deletes its writable layer, not the image.

docker-images.title: A cache-friendly Dockerfile
docker-images.code:
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt   # cached until requirements change
COPY . .                                            # code changes only rebuild from here
USER 1000
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
docker-images.explanation: Copy the dependency file and install before copying source code, so editing code does not reinstall every package.

docker-run.title: Common run options
docker-run.code:
docker run -d \
  --name api \
  -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000 \
  -e DATABASE_URL=postgres://db:5432/app \
  --restart unless-stopped \
  --memory 512m --cpus 1 \
  myorg/api:1.4.2
docker-run.explanation: Binding to 127.0.0.1 keeps the port off the public interface; limits stop one container starving the host; pin an image tag rather than latest.

docker-data-net.title: Named volume and user-defined network
docker-data-net.code:
docker network create appnet
docker volume create pgdata
docker run -d --name db --network appnet -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data \
  -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE=/run/secrets/pg postgres:16
docker run -d --name api --network appnet myorg/api:1.4.2
# inside api, the database is reachable at host name 'db'
docker-data-net.explanation: Containers on a user-defined network resolve each other by name (the default bridge does not), and the named volume keeps data when the db container is replaced.

docker-compose.title: A compose file with a health check
docker-compose.code:
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    volumes: [pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data]
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
  api:
    build: .
    ports: ["8000:8000"]
    depends_on:
      db: { condition: service_healthy }
volumes:
  pgdata:
docker-compose.explanation: depends_on with service_healthy waits until the database actually accepts connections, not just until its container has started.

docker-registry.title: Tag and push to a registry
docker-registry.code:
docker build -t myorg/api:1.4.2 .
docker tag myorg/api:1.4.2 ghcr.io/myorg/api:1.4.2
echo $GHCR_TOKEN | docker login ghcr.io -u myorg --password-stdin
docker push ghcr.io/myorg/api:1.4.2
docker buildx imagetools inspect ghcr.io/myorg/api:1.4.2   # shows the digest
docker-registry.explanation: The registry host is part of the image name. Deploy by digest (@sha256:...) for an immutable reference; tags can be moved.

docker-optimization-security.title: Multi-stage build to a minimal image
docker-optimization-security.code:
FROM golang:1.23 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /out/app .

FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot
COPY --from=build /out/app /app
USER nonroot
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]
docker-optimization-security.explanation: The compiler and source stay in the build stage; the final image holds only the binary, runs as non-root and has no shell, so it is tiny with few CVEs to scan.

docker-ops.title: Debug a container that keeps restarting
docker-ops.code:
$ docker ps -a --filter name=api
api   Restarting (1) 3 seconds ago
$ docker logs --tail 20 api
Error: connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:5432
$ docker inspect -f '{{.State.ExitCode}} {{.RestartCount}}' api
1 14
docker-ops.explanation: Logs show the app trying localhost: inside a container that is the container itself, not the database. Point it at the db service name instead.

git-basics.title: First repository
git-basics.code:
$ git init demo && cd demo
$ echo '# Demo' > README.md
$ git status --short
?? README.md
$ git add README.md
$ git commit -m "Add README"
$ git log --oneline
a1b2c3d Add README
git-basics.explanation: Files move from untracked to staged (git add) to committed (git commit). git status tells you which state each file is in.

git-staging-commits.title: Stage part of a change
git-staging-commits.code:
$ git add -p app.py          # choose hunks: y = stage, n = skip
$ git diff --staged          # what will be committed
$ git diff                   # what is still unstaged
$ git commit -m "Fix rounding in invoice totals"
git-staging-commits.explanation: Interactive staging lets one messy working session become several focused commits, each with a clear message.

git-remotes.title: Fetch, inspect, then integrate
git-remotes.code:
$ git fetch origin
$ git log --oneline main..origin/main     # commits you don't have yet
4e5f6a7 Update dependencies
$ git merge --ff-only origin/main         # or: git pull --rebase
$ git push -u origin feature/login        # set upstream on first push
git-remotes.explanation: fetch is always safe: it downloads without touching your branches, so you can look before you merge.

git-branching.title: Feature branch lifecycle
git-branching.code:
$ git switch -c feature/search
# ...commits...
$ git switch main && git pull
$ git merge --no-ff feature/search
$ git branch -d feature/search
$ git log --oneline --graph -5
git-branching.explanation: Branches are cheap pointers to commits. --no-ff keeps a merge commit so the feature remains visible as a unit in history.

git-conflicts.title: Resolve a merge conflict
git-conflicts.code:
<<<<<<< HEAD
TIMEOUT = 30
=======
TIMEOUT = 60
>>>>>>> feature/slow-api

# edit to the intended result, remove the markers:
TIMEOUT = 60
$ git add config.py && git commit
git-conflicts.explanation: Git marks both versions; you decide the correct result, then stage it to mark the conflict resolved. Run the tests before committing.

git-undo.title: Pick the right undo
git-undo.code:
Situation                                 Command
----------------------------------------  -------------------------------
Discard unstaged edits to a file          git restore app.py
Unstage a file                            git restore --staged app.py
Fix the last unpushed commit message      git commit --amend
Undo a pushed commit safely               git revert <sha>
Find a 'lost' commit after a reset        git reflog
git-undo.explanation: Rewrite only unpushed history; for anything shared, revert creates a new commit that undoes the change.

git-workflows.title: Trunk-based flow with a pull request
git-workflows.code:
$ git switch -c fix/null-total main
$ git commit -am "Handle empty cart total"
$ git push -u origin fix/null-total
# open PR -> CI runs tests -> review -> squash merge to main within a day
$ git switch main && git pull && git branch -d fix/null-total
git-workflows.explanation: Short-lived branches merged daily keep conflicts small; unfinished features hide behind flags rather than long-lived branches.

git-internals-hygiene.title: Look inside a commit object
git-internals-hygiene.code:
$ git cat-file -p HEAD
tree 9b2c...
parent 4e5f...
author Ana <ana@example.com> 1715500000 +0000
committer Ana <ana@example.com> 1715500000 +0000

Add README
$ git cat-file -p 9b2c...
100644 blob 7d1e...    README.md
git-internals-hygiene.explanation: A commit points to a tree (a directory listing), which points to blobs (file contents), all addressed by hash. Change any byte and every hash above it changes.

k8s-basics.title: Explore a cluster
k8s-basics.code:
$ kubectl get nodes
NAME     STATUS   ROLES           VERSION
cp-1     Ready    control-plane   v1.31.2
work-1   Ready    <none>          v1.31.2
$ kubectl get pods -A
$ kubectl describe pod web-7c9d-abc12   # events explain scheduling and pull errors
$ kubectl explain deployment.spec.replicas
k8s-basics.explanation: get lists, describe explains (including events), and explain documents any field without leaving the terminal.

k8s-workloads.title: A Deployment
k8s-workloads.explanation: The Deployment manages a ReplicaSet that keeps three pods running; delete one and a replacement is created.

k8s-config.title: ConfigMap and Secret as environment
k8s-config.code:
kubectl create configmap app-cfg --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=info
kubectl create secret generic db --from-literal=PASSWORD='s3cr3t'

# in the pod spec:
envFrom:
- configMapRef: { name: app-cfg }
env:
- name: DB_PASSWORD
  valueFrom: { secretKeyRef: { name: db, key: PASSWORD } }
k8s-config.explanation: Secrets are only base64-encoded by default; enable encryption at rest for etcd and restrict who can read them with RBAC.

k8s-networking.title: Service and Ingress
k8s-networking.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: web }
spec:
  selector: { app: web }
  ports: [{ port: 80, targetPort: 80 }]
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata: { name: web }
spec:
  rules:
  - host: shop.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - { path: /, pathType: Prefix, backend: { service: { name: web, port: { number: 80 } } } }
k8s-networking.explanation: The Service gives pods a stable name and IP (web.<namespace>.svc); the Ingress routes external HTTP by host and path to it. An ingress controller must be installed.

k8s-storage.title: PersistentVolumeClaim
k8s-storage.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata: { name: data }
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  storageClassName: standard
  resources: { requests: { storage: 10Gi } }
---
# pod spec
volumes: [{ name: data, persistentVolumeClaim: { claimName: data } }]
containers: [{ name: db, image: postgres:16, volumeMounts: [{ name: data, mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data }] }]
k8s-storage.explanation: The claim asks for storage; the StorageClass provisions a volume dynamically. Data survives pod restarts and rescheduling.

k8s-deployments.title: Roll out and roll back
k8s-deployments.code:
$ kubectl set image deploy/web web=nginx:1.27.1
$ kubectl rollout status deploy/web
Waiting for deployment "web" rollout to finish: 1 of 3 updated replicas are available...
$ kubectl rollout history deploy/web
$ kubectl rollout undo deploy/web          # back to the previous ReplicaSet
k8s-deployments.explanation: Rolling updates replace pods gradually, gated by readiness probes; a bad version can be undone in one command.

k8s-operations.title: Drain a node for maintenance
k8s-operations.code:
$ kubectl cordon work-1                 # no new pods scheduled here
$ kubectl drain work-1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
# ...patch and reboot...
$ kubectl uncordon work-1
k8s-operations.explanation: Drain evicts pods so controllers recreate them elsewhere, respecting PodDisruptionBudgets so the service stays up.

k8s-security.title: Least-privilege RBAC and a restricted pod
k8s-security.code:
kind: Role
metadata: { name: read-pods, namespace: shop }
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods", "pods/log"]
  verbs: ["get", "list"]
---
# namespace label for Pod Security Admission
pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted
# containers then must run as non-root, drop ALL capabilities, no privilege escalation
k8s-security.explanation: Roles grant only the verbs needed in one namespace; the restricted Pod Security Standard blocks risky pod settings at admission.

sql-basics.title: Create, insert and query
sql-basics.explanation: Tables have typed columns and a primary key that uniquely identifies each row.

sql-select.title: Filter, sort and limit
sql-select.code:
SELECT name, total
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid'
  AND created_at >= '2026-01-01'
  AND coupon IS NULL          -- not '= NULL'
ORDER BY total DESC
LIMIT 5;
sql-select.explanation: NULL is never equal to anything, including NULL, so use IS NULL. Clauses are written SELECT-FROM-WHERE-ORDER BY but evaluated FROM first.

sql-aggregates.title: GROUP BY with HAVING
sql-aggregates.code:
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(total) AS spent
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid'          -- filters rows before grouping
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(total) > 1000       -- filters groups after
ORDER BY spent DESC;
sql-aggregates.explanation: WHERE cannot use aggregates because it runs before grouping; HAVING runs after and can.

sql-joins.title: INNER vs LEFT JOIN
sql-joins.code:
-- customers: Ana(1), Ben(2), Cy(3); orders exist for 1 and 2 only
SELECT c.name, o.id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id;
-- Ana 101 | Ben 102 | Cy NULL

-- customers with no orders:
... LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL;   -- Cy
sql-joins.explanation: INNER JOIN keeps only matches; LEFT JOIN keeps every left row and fills NULLs, which makes 'find the missing ones' queries easy.

sql-ddl-dml.title: Safe UPDATE
sql-ddl-dml.explanation: An UPDATE or DELETE without WHERE changes every row. Previewing with SELECT inside a transaction lets you check the count before committing.

sql-subqueries.title: Subquery and CTE
sql-subqueries.code:
-- customers who spent more than average
WITH spend AS (
  SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) AS spent
  FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT customer_id, spent
FROM spend
WHERE spent > (SELECT AVG(spent) FROM spend);
sql-subqueries.explanation: A CTE names an intermediate result so the query reads top to bottom; the scalar subquery computes the average once for comparison.

sql-indexes-norm.title: See an index change the plan
sql-indexes-norm.explanation: Without an index the database reads every row; with it, it jumps to the matches. Indexes speed reads but slow writes, so add them for real query patterns.

sql-transactions-security.title: Atomic transfer with least-privilege user
sql-transactions-security.explanation: The transaction makes the transfer atomic; the application account gets only the privileges it needs, limiting the damage of SQL injection.

tf-iac-basics.title: Declare, plan, apply
tf-iac-basics.explanation: You declare the desired end state; Terraform compares it with the state file and real infrastructure and shows the plan before changing anything.

tf-core-workflow.title: Plan file in CI
tf-core-workflow.code:
terraform fmt -check
terraform validate
terraform plan -out=tfplan
terraform show -no-color tfplan > plan.txt   # attach to the PR for review
terraform apply tfplan                      # applies exactly what was reviewed
tf-core-workflow.explanation: Saving the plan guarantees the apply matches what reviewers approved, even if the code or cloud changed in between.

tf-resources.title: References create dependencies
tf-resources.explanation: Referencing aws_vpc.main.id tells Terraform to create the VPC first. Data sources read existing objects without managing them.

tf-variables.title: Typed variable with validation
tf-variables.explanation: Validation fails fast on bad input. sensitive hides values from output but not from state, so protect the state file.

tf-expressions.title: for_each over a map
tf-expressions.explanation: for_each keys instances by name (aws_s3_bucket.b["logs"]), so removing one entry does not shift or recreate the others, unlike count.

tf-state-backends.title: Remote state with S3-native locking
tf-state-backends.explanation: Shared, encrypted remote state lets a team work safely; the lock stops two applies running at once. Enable bucket versioning to recover from mistakes.

tf-modules.title: Call a versioned module
tf-modules.explanation: Pinning the module version means upgrades are deliberate; module outputs are read as module.<name>.<output>.

tf-meta-lifecycle.title: Lifecycle rules
tf-meta-lifecycle.explanation: prevent_destroy protects stateful resources from an accidental replace; create_before_destroy avoids downtime when a resource must be recreated.

tf-prod-security.title: Scan and gate a plan
tf-prod-security.code:
$ terraform plan -out=tfplan && terraform show -json tfplan > plan.json
$ checkov -f plan.json
Check: CKV_AWS_18 "Ensure the S3 bucket has access logging enabled"
  FAILED for resource: aws_s3_bucket.logs
$ trivy config .
tf-prod-security.explanation: Policy scanners catch insecure settings before apply. Run them in the pipeline and use OIDC roles for CI instead of stored cloud keys.

go-types.title: Structs, methods and interfaces
go-types.explanation: Rect satisfies Shape implicitly by having an Area method; Go has no 'implements' keyword.

rust-types.title: Enums and exhaustive match
rust-types.explanation: match must cover every variant, so adding a new payment type is a compile error until each match handles it.

it-what-is-it.title: Follow one request through IT
it-what-is-it.code:
You open shop.example.com on a laptop
 Hardware    laptop CPU, RAM, Wi-Fi card
 Software    browser on the operating system
 Network     Wi-Fi -> router -> ISP -> internet (DNS finds the server)
 Server      web app and database in a data centre or cloud
 Security    HTTPS encrypts the page and your password
 Support     help desk resets the password you forgot
it-what-is-it.explanation: Every IT role looks after one piece of this chain; a problem anywhere breaks the whole experience.

it-hardware.title: Read a spec sheet
it-hardware.code:
CPU:      8 cores / 16 threads, 3.8 GHz, x86-64
RAM:      16 GB DDR5
Storage:  1 TB NVMe SSD
GPU:      integrated
Network:  Wi-Fi 6E, 2.5 GbE
PSU:      650 W
it-hardware.explanation: Cores and threads decide how much runs at once, RAM how much is held in fast memory, and the SSD how quickly programs load.

it-storage-memory.title: Why a 1 TB drive shows 931 GB
it-storage-memory.code:
Manufacturer:  1 TB  = 1,000,000,000,000 bytes (decimal)
Windows shows: 1,000,000,000,000 / 1,073,741,824 = 931.3 'GB'
               (really 931.3 GiB, binary units)
it-storage-memory.explanation: Nothing is missing: drive makers count in powers of 10 and Windows in powers of 2 while still printing 'GB'.

it-os-boot.title: The UEFI boot sequence
it-os-boot.code:
1. Power on -> firmware (UEFI) runs POST hardware checks
2. UEFI reads boot entries from NVRAM, finds the EFI System Partition (GPT disk)
3. Secure Boot verifies the bootloader's signature
4. Bootloader (Windows Boot Manager / GRUB) loads the kernel
5. Kernel starts drivers and the first process (init / systemd, or wininit)
6. Services start -> login screen
it-os-boot.explanation: Knowing the order tells you where a failure is: no POST beep is hardware, 'no boot device' is firmware or disk, a crash after the logo is the OS.

net-osi.title: Troubleshoot layer by layer
net-osi.code:
Layer 1  link light on? cable/Wi-Fi connected?
Layer 2  ip link / arp -a        MAC addresses seen?
Layer 3  ping 192.168.1.1        reach the gateway? ping 1.1.1.1
Layer 4  Test-NetConnection shop.example.com -Port 443
Layer 7  nslookup shop.example.com ; curl -I https://shop.example.com
net-osi.explanation: Work bottom-up: if you can ping 1.1.1.1 but not a name, the problem is DNS, not the cable.

net-devices-media.title: Switch MAC table vs router route table
net-devices-media.code:
Switch# show mac address-table
Vlan  Mac Address       Type     Ports
10    a4bb.6d12.3401    DYNAMIC  Gi0/3

Router# show ip route
C   192.168.10.0/24 is directly connected, Gi0/0
S*  0.0.0.0/0 [1/0] via 203.0.113.1
net-devices-media.explanation: A switch forwards frames by MAC address within a network; a router forwards packets by IP address between networks.

net-ops.title: Find where traffic stops
net-ops.code:
$ traceroute -n 8.8.8.8
 1  192.168.1.1   1.1 ms
 2  10.20.0.1     8.4 ms
 3  * * *
 4  * * *
$ mtr -rwc 50 8.8.8.8      # loss per hop over 50 probes
net-ops.explanation: Timeouts at one hop that continue onward are often just ICMP rate limiting; loss that persists to the destination points to a real problem at or after that hop.

rt-fundamentals.title: Longest prefix match
rt-fundamentals.explanation: The most specific matching prefix wins; administrative distance only decides between the same prefix learned from different sources.

rt-isis.title: A minimal IS-IS configuration
rt-isis.code:
router isis CORE
 net 49.0001.1921.6800.1001.00     ! area 49.0001, system ID 1921.6800.1001
 is-type level-2-only
 metric-style wide
!
interface Gi0/0
 ip router isis CORE
 isis network point-to-point
rt-isis.explanation: The NET encodes the area and a unique system ID. IS-IS runs directly over Layer 2, not IP, which is one reason large ISPs favour it.

rt-routing-security.title: Check a route's RPKI validity
rt-routing-security.code:
ROA:  prefix 203.0.113.0/24, max length /24, origin AS64500

Announcement                 Origin    Result
---------------------------  --------  ---------
203.0.113.0/24               AS64500   Valid
203.0.113.0/24               AS64666   Invalid (wrong origin) -> drop
203.0.113.128/25             AS64500   Invalid (longer than max length)
198.51.100.0/24              AS64510   NotFound (no ROA)
rt-routing-security.explanation: Route origin validation (RFC 6811) rejects hijacks from the wrong AS and more-specific announcements; MANRS asks networks to filter Invalid routes.
